newsitem.title: NETHERLANDS: Reed Elsevier's Lexis-Nexis targets Europe.
newsitem.headline: Reed Elsevier's Lexis-Nexis targets Europe.

text.p: Anglo-Dutch publishing group Reed Elsevier said on Wednesday its Lexis-Nexis on-line information unit was stepping up efforts to expand outside its U.S. base and particularly in Europe.
Co-chairman Herman Bruggink told an annual results presentation that a separate European Lexis-Nexis operation had been set up in London under Dutch manager Hans Giesink.
"He is now in charge of developing Lexis-Nexis in all the countries of Europe by hiring staff, adding local content.... I'm very optimistic about the outlook for Lexis-Nexis in Europe," he said.
"Lexis-Nexis when we bought it (in 1994) was trying to conquer the world from Dayton, Ohio. Now we have an organisation, with Reed Elsevier, that is based all over the world," he added.
Lexis-Nexis -- which supplies legal, government and general information -- saw its operating profits rise 29 percent in 1996. Its operating margin rose to 23 percent from 20 percent.

Bruggink said Reed Elsevier planned to accelerate the development of new products and services in 1997, particularly in the area of electronic publishing. New technology would allow the group to achieve higher rates of organic growth, he said.

"We believe we can increase and improve the growth, the dynamics, of our existing business more than we did in the past. And that is because of the promising future of electronic publishing," Bruggink said.
Reed Elsevier plans to launch its Science Direct electronic delivery platform for scientific journals by mid-1997.
Bruggink said he hoped this would spur on the development of electronic delivery formats in science publishing, saying they were currently a small part of the business but growing fast.
Science publishing is Reed Elsevier's most profitable business with an operating margin of 41.8 percent in 1996.
Bruggink said that in addition to seeking double-digit organic growth, Reed Elsevier would continue to pursue an active acquisitions policy.
"We need them and we are continuing to look for those large acquistions," he said.
However, the pace of acquisitions was beyond Reed Elsevier's control, much as a farmer could not control the rain, he said.
"Acquisitions are rain. You cannot run and grow the business without acquisitions...but sometimes rain comes, sometimes it doesn't," he said.
